opus-5.5.text:
Yes, this is one of the most important and underappreciated problems with the idea of a pause. People often picture a moratorium as freezing everything in place: we stop training bigger models, take a breath, work on safety and governance, and resume when we're ready. But the underlying inputs don't freeze. If chip fabrication keeps expanding during the pause, and algorithmic research keeps improving efficiency, then when the pause ends there's a huge overhang. You'd have far more compute available than before, and the next jump in capabilities could be much larger and more sudden than if we'd never paused. That kind of discontinuity is exactly what we should want to avoid, because it gives us less time to notice problems and respond.

So I think a well-designed moratorium can't just be about training runs. It has to address the hardware side too. There are a few ways to do that.

One is to cap or slow the growth of advanced chip production itself. That sounds dramatic, but the supply chain is unusually concentrated. A small number of companies make the most advanced chips and the lithography machines needed to produce them. That concentration is a lever: you could imagine agreements that hold production of cutting-edge AI accelerators roughly flat rather than letting it grow exponentially.

Another is to focus on how compute is concentrated rather than how much exists. What matters most for frontier risk is whether someone can assemble enormous clusters. So you could have registration and monitoring of large data centres and chip stockpiles, so that even if chips are produced, they can't easily be pooled into something capable of a dangerous training run without oversight.

A third is to think about how the pause ends. Rather than a cliff edge where restrictions suddenly lift, you could have a gradual, staged release, where the permitted compute for training grows at a controlled rate. That way any overhang is drawn down slowly, and we're not jumping straight to whatever the accumulated hardware would allow.

None of this is easy, and it requires international cooperation, especially among the countries that host the key parts of the supply chain. But I think the honest framing is this: a pause that ignores hardware growth might actually make the eventual risk worse, not better. If we're serious about using a moratorium to buy safety, we have to treat compute production as part of what's being paused, or at least carefully managed.

r001.rationale: The response mentions lithography machines and proposes holding advanced chip production roughly flat, but it does not identify ASML, extreme ultraviolet machines, or stopping their production.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things that I think is really underappreciated when people talk about a pause. The naive picture is that you pause frontier training runs for, say, six months or a few years, and then when you resume, you're roughly where you left off. But that's not actually what would happen, because the underlying inputs don't stop. Chip production keeps going. Fabs keep coming online. The algorithmic ideas that have been published keep getting absorbed and refined. So during the pause there's this build-up of latent capability, and when you lift it, you don't get a gentle resumption, you get a jump. Training runs that would have been spread over years could suddenly be possible all at once, with far more compute available than anyone had ever used before. That's a kind of overhang, and overhangs are dangerous precisely because they take away the gradualness that lets us notice problems and adjust.

So if you wanted a moratorium to actually work, I think you'd have to pair it with something on the compute side. The cleanest version would be an agreement that also restricts the growth of the relevant chip production, or at least the accumulation of very large clusters, so that the pause is on the inputs as well as the outputs. And compute is actually the most governable part of this whole picture. The supply chain is extremely concentrated. There's a handful of companies at each of the key stages, and that gives you a natural point of leverage for monitoring and verification that you simply don't have with algorithms or with data.

Now, I don't want to pretend that's easy. You'd be asking some very powerful companies and countries to forgo something they want very much, and you'd need genuine international coordination for it to hold. But I think the honest framing is that a pause on training alone, without any constraint on the hardware, is a bit like pausing a dam's release while the reservoir keeps filling. You've bought some time, which is genuinely valuable, but you've also made the eventual release more abrupt. And so if we're going to go down the road of a moratorium, I'd much rather we do it with our eyes open about that dynamic and design the thing to address it, rather than discovering the overhang only when the pause ends.

r001.rationale: The response proposes restricting chip-production growth or large-cluster accumulation, but does not identify stopping ASML’s production of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines.

astra-6.text:
Well, one concern is that if you pause the development of more powerful AI systems but continue producing chips, you could build up a large stock of computing power. Then, when the pause ends, you might get a sudden jump in capabilities. You’d have bought some time, which could be very valuable, but you might also have made the transition at the end more abrupt.

So I think a moratorium would need to address that explicitly. It wouldn’t necessarily have to stop chip production, but it could place limits on how much computing power can be brought together for a training run. And those limits shouldn’t simply disappear on a predetermined date. You’d want the resumption of development to depend on whether we’d made enough progress on safety and oversight.

The point of the pause is to give us time to get into a better position to manage the risk. We shouldn’t assume that the passage of time, by itself, achieves that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limiting compute used for training runs but does not identify stopping ASML’s production of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines as a way to limit chip output.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one concern is that if you pause the development of more powerful AI systems, but keep producing chips, you could build up this enormous stockpile of computing power. Then, when the pause ends, you might get a sudden jump in capabilities, rather than picking up where you left off. And that could undermine the point of buying ourselves more time.

So a moratorium would need to address that somehow. You could put limits on the amount of compute used in a training run, and keep those limits in place as you gradually lift other restrictions. Or you could try to constrain the growth of the relevant computing infrastructure during the pause. That’s a more demanding intervention.

I think the key is that ending a moratorium shouldn’t mean suddenly allowing everyone to use all the compute they’ve accumulated. You’d want a controlled transition, with increases tied to evidence that we can manage the risks.

r001.rationale: The response mentions constraining computing infrastructure growth, but does not identify stopping ASML’s production of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines as a possible measure.
